question.text: An investor has a 15-year retirement goal. His financial adviser suggests "time in the market" rather than "timing the market." This advice implies:

answer.text: The investor should invest only when markets are at their lowest
The investor should switch between equity and debt based on market levels
Staying invested consistently over long periods is more important than trying to predict market highs and lows
The investor should redeem and re-enter the market frequently to capture short-term gains

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook supports systematic investing without trying to predict market movements and treats equities as suitable for long investment horizons such as a 15-year retirement goal. SIP / rupee-cost averaging is presented as a way to smooth volatility, while frequent switching brings switching costs and tax friction. These points together favour staying invested over trying to time the market. The Trap: Investing only at market lows is itself market timing and is hard to execute consistently. Switching between asset classes on market views is also timing, and frequent redemption and re-entry adds transaction costs and tax costs while running the risk of being out of the market during sharp moves. Note: The explanation avoids specific quantitative claims (such as missing the best ten days or 40-50 percent return reduction) since those are not directly supported on the workbook pages checked; the qualitative case for time in the market is sufficient.
